heading: Overview
content: Prompt caching optimizes API usage by allowing resuming from specific prefixes in prompts, significantly reducing processing time and costs for repetitive tasks or prompts with consistent elements. The feature is eligible for Zero Data Retention (ZDR); when an organization has a ZDR arrangement, data sent through this feature is not stored after the API response is returned. Two ways to enable it: Automatic caching adds a single cache_control field at the top level of the request, and the system automatically applies the cache breakpoint to the last cacheable block and moves it forward as conversations grow, best for multi-turn conversations. Explicit cache breakpoints place cache_control directly on individual content blocks for fine-grained control over exactly what gets cached. With automatic caching, the system caches all content up to and including the last cacheable block, and cached content is reused automatically on subsequent requests with the same prefix.

heading: How Prompt Caching Works
content: When a request with prompt caching enabled is sent: the system checks if a prompt prefix, up to a specified cache breakpoint, is already cached from a recent query; if found, it uses the cached version, reducing processing time and costs; otherwise it processes the full prompt and caches the prefix once the response begins. Especially useful for prompts with many examples, large amounts of context or background information, repetitive tasks with consistent instructions, and long multi-turn conversations. By default the cache has a 5-minute lifetime, refreshed for no additional cost each time the cached content is used; a 1-hour cache duration is available at additional cost. Prompt caching caches the full prefix: it references the entire prompt, tools, system, and messages in that order, up to and including the block designated with cache_control.

heading: Pricing
content: Price per million tokens by model: Claude Opus 4.8/4.7/4.6/4.5 are $5 base input, $6.25 5-minute cache write, $10 1-hour cache write, $0.50 cache hits/refreshes, $25 output tokens (all per MTok). Claude Opus 4.1 and the deprecated Opus 4 are $15 base input, $18.75 5-minute write, $30 1-hour write, $1.50 cache hits, $75 output. Claude Sonnet 4.6/4.5 and deprecated Sonnet 4 are $3 base input, $3.75 5-minute write, $6 1-hour write, $0.30 cache hits, $15 output. Claude Haiku 4.5 is $1 base input, $1.25 5-minute write, $2 1-hour write, $0.10 cache hits, $5 output. Claude Haiku 3.5 (retired except on Bedrock and Vertex AI) is $0.80 base input, $1 5-minute write, $1.60 1-hour write, $0.08 cache hits, $4 output. Pricing multipliers: 5-minute cache write tokens are 1.25x base input token price; 1-hour cache write tokens are 2x base input token price; cache read tokens are 0.1x base input token price. These multipliers stack with other pricing modifiers such as the Batch API discount and data residency.

heading: Supported Models
content: Prompt caching, both automatic and explicit, is supported on all active Claude models.

heading: Automatic Caching Mechanics and Multi-Turn Behavior
content: Automatic caching is enabled by adding a single cache_control field at the top level of the request body rather than placing it on individual content blocks; the system automatically applies the cache breakpoint to the last cacheable block. In multi-turn conversations, the cache point moves forward automatically as conversations grow: Request 1 writes everything (System, User1, Asst1, User2) to cache; Request 2 reads System through User2 from cache and writes Asst2 plus User3; Request 3 reads System through User3 from cache and writes Asst3 plus User4. The cache breakpoint automatically moves to the last cacheable block in each request, so cache_control markers never need manual updating as the conversation grows. TTL support: by default automatic caching uses a 5-minute TTL, but a 1-hour TTL can be specified at 2x the base input token price via cache_control: {type: ephemeral, ttl: 1h}. Automatic caching is compatible with explicit cache breakpoints; when used together, the automatic cache breakpoint uses one of the 4 available breakpoint slots, e.g. an explicit breakpoint can cache the system prompt while automatic caching handles the conversation. What stays the same: automatic caching uses the same underlying caching infrastructure, and pricing, minimum token thresholds, context ordering requirements, and the 20-block lookback window all apply the same as with explicit breakpoints.
